tagline: Lead the the team that detects and warns about arial threats
overview: As an Air Defense Artillery (ADA) Officer, you’ll lead the air defense artillery branch at all levels of command. You’ll manage modern complicated military computers on complex networks, communications equipment systems, and radars in order to provide warning, detection, and protection for armed forces from aerial attack, missile attack, and aerial surveillance.

ai.blurb: Commands Army units that use radar and missile systems to spot, track and shoot down aircraft, drones and incoming missiles.
ai.dayToDay: You lead a platoon or battery of soldiers running radars, launchers and the networks that tie them together, often from a command post full of screens and radio traffic. Much of the work is planning coverage, running drills, keeping expensive equipment serviceable and briefing higher headquarters — punctuated by field exercises and deployments where crews stand watch around the clock. Expect to spend as much time on maintenance reports and personnel problems as on the tactical picture.

title: Patriot Fire Control Enhanced Operator / Maintainer
tagline: Track targets and fire antiaircraft missiles
overview: As a Patriot Fire Control Enhanced Operator / Maintainer, you’ll be responsible for operating and maintaining the four major parts of the Patriot Fire Control system. You’ll act quickly and with precision to identify, track, and engage those identified threats using one of the world’s most advanced interceptor missile systems capable of destroying enemy air threats at a moment’s notice. Soldiers in this branch will enlist as an Air Defense Artillery (ADA) Soldier ([14U](https://www.goarmy.com/careers-and-jobs/aviation/detecting-aerial-threats/14u-air-defense-artillery-recruit)) and be assigned to a specific ADA job (14-Series MOS) based on available Army opportunities and skills assessed at Basic Combat Training.
requirements: Eligible for a Secret Security Clearance

ai.blurb: Operates and maintains the Patriot missile system, spotting aircraft and missiles on radar and engaging them.
ai.dayToDay: Much of the work happens inside a cramped engagement control station — screens, radios, air conditioning and a lot of waiting broken by sudden urgency. You train on the consoles, run drills, and spend plenty of hours outside maintaining radars, launchers and generators, hauling cables and driving the heavy vehicles that carry it all. Patriot units deploy often to places where air threats are real, and you work as a tight crew where one person's mistake is everyone's problem.
ai.funFact: Patriot is usually explained as standing for Phased Array Tracking Radar to Intercept of Target — a backronym that was clearly reverse-engineered to spell something patriotic.
goodFitIf: You stay calm under time pressure
You like radar screens and wrenches equally
You can tolerate long quiet stretches
You want a Secret clearance

title: Air Defense Battle Management System Operator
tagline: Spot aerial threats
overview: As an Air Defense Battle Management System Operator, you’ll use specialized skills to sustain air space superiority and protect against aerial and missile attacks by providing critical situational awareness, threat detection, and early warnings from airspace. Spotting an incoming threat in advance can be a crucial advantage in protecting ground forces and provide overall ease for many Soldiers. Additionally, you’ll learn to evaluate intelligence data, maintain and troubleshoot systems, and establish connectivity to air defense networks. Soldiers in this branch will enlist as an Air Defense Artillery (ADA) Soldier ([14U](https://www.goarmy.com/careers-and-jobs/aviation/detecting-aerial-threats/14u-air-defense-artillery-recruit)) and be assigned to a specific ADA job (14-Series MOS) based on available Army opportunities and skills assessed at Basic Combat Training.

Screens and data don't bore you
You like fixing electronics as well as using them
You can hold a Secret clearance

You’ll train to read temperature and pressure gauges, make operating adjustments to utility equipment, test for leaks, perform preventative maintenance, troubleshoot malfunctions, and read and use technical manuals and diagnostic instruments.

ai.blurb: Keeps air conditioners, refrigeration units and other utility equipment running, from base buildings to field camps.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work is hands-on troubleshooting: reading temperature and pressure gauges, checking for refrigerant leaks, tracing circuits and wiring, and doing scheduled preventative maintenance before something fails. You'll spend time in maintenance shops and on site wherever the equipment lives — motor pools, field kitchens, medical units, climate-controlled shelters — often with a technical manual open beside you. Pace swings between routine servicing and urgent calls when a cooling unit quits in a bad place at a bad time.
ai.funFact: Refrigeration is quietly a combat-relevant trade: field hospitals, blood supplies and vaccines all depend on cold chains, which is why HVAC technicians deploy alongside everyone else.

You're comfortable with tools and gauges
You can follow a technical manual carefully
Heat, cold and dirt don't bother you

You’ll supervise and manage the reception, storage, and shipping of bulk or packaged petroleum-based products. You’ll oversee its use, dispense it to various vehicles and aircraft, and make sure it is being transported and handled safely. You will learn how refueling systems and equipment are assembled sequentially, perform quality assurance, and you’ll supply and store fuel from a variety of sources.

ai.blurb: Receives, stores, tests and pumps the fuel that keeps Army vehicles, aircraft and generators running.
ai.dayToDay: You'll work around tanks, pumps, hoses and fuel trucks — on a motor pool, a flight line, or a field site where you've just helped assemble a refuelling system from scratch. Days mix physical work (dragging hoses, hooking up couplings, filling vehicles) with careful paperwork: logging quantities, running quality checks on samples, and scheduling deliveries. It's outdoors, often early, usually in a small team, and safety rules are taken very seriously because the product is flammable.
ai.funFact: Fuel handlers are among the few Soldiers who routinely refuel helicopters with the rotors still turning — a procedure known as hot refuelling.

title: Culinary Specialist

overview: As a Culinary Specialist, you’ll cook meals and work alongside chefs to prepare meals comparable to any major restaurant, so that Soldiers can sit down and enjoy a hot meal in between training or mission deployments. You’ll be responsible for preparing and servicing meals both in the field and at home stations, as well as ordering, inspecting food supplies, and keeping the kitchen safe and sanitary.

ai.blurb: Cooks and serves meals for Soldiers, in garrison kitchens and out in the field, and keeps the food supply safe.
ai.dayToDay: Early starts are the norm — breakfast doesn't cook itself. You'll work in a dining facility kitchen or a field kitchen on exercise, prepping and cooking in bulk alongside other cooks and senior food service NCOs, then cleaning down and doing it again. Beyond cooking there's ordering stock, inspecting deliveries, rotating storage and meeting sanitation standards, which matters more when hundreds of people eat what you made.
ai.funFact: Army cooks have long been known informally as "cooks" long before the branch renamed the job Culinary Specialist, and the Army runs an annual culinary arts competition where teams compete at a genuinely serious level.

title: Mortuary Affairs Specialist
tagline: Handle remains and arrange funerals
overview: As a Mortuary Affairs Specialist, you'll draw upon specialized medical training and the utmost respect and compassion to handle the remains and personal effects of Soldiers who have fallen in the line of duty. This includes locating and identifying remains in the field, ensuring safe transport of the deceased and their belongings, and assisting with arrangements and military honors at their burial site. You'll also inventory and safeguard effects and serve as a specialist at the U.S. Army’s Central Identification Laboratory in Hawaii.
requirements: Be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident with a valid Green Card

ai.blurb: Recovers, identifies and cares for the remains and personal belongings of service members who die in the line of duty.
ai.dayToDay: Work ranges from a collection point in the field, searching for and recovering remains, to a processing facility where you inventory personal effects and prepare the deceased for transport home. There's careful paperwork and chain-of-custody documentation alongside the physical work, and you may assist with burial arrangements and military honours. Some 92Ms serve at the Army's Central Identification Laboratory in Hawaii, which works on identifying remains from past conflicts.
ai.funFact: Mortuary affairs is one of the Army's smallest specialities, and its people take the view that every fallen service member is brought home — identification work on remains from past wars continues decades later.
goodFitIf: You can stay steady under grim conditions
You're meticulous about records and detail
You treat other people's families with respect
You're interested in forensic or funeral work

title: Parachute Rigger
tagline: Inspect, test and pack parachutes
overview: As a Parachute Rigger, you’ll ensure the safety of every paratrooper you work with. You’ll inspect, test, and pack parachutes, their extraction and release systems, and all the associated components of the parachute system. You’ll be responsible for the safety and repair of all parachute equipment before, during, and after an airdrop operation. You’ll be responsible for assembling rigging components and securing all the supplies in the aircraft.
requirements: Be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident with a valid Green Card

ai.blurb: Packs, inspects and repairs the parachutes that soldiers and cargo depend on to land in one piece.
ai.dayToDay: Most of the work happens in a rigger shed — long tables, sewing machines, and a packing floor where canopies are laid out, checked panel by panel and folded to an exact sequence. You'll also rig pallets and vehicles for airdrop, load them onto aircraft, and recover and repair the gear afterwards. It's methodical, repetitive and checked constantly, because a missed detail has obvious consequences.
ai.funFact: Riggers traditionally jump with chutes they packed themselves — the oldest and bluntest quality-assurance system in the Army.
goodFitIf: You're meticulous about small details
You like working with your hands
You can stay calm doing repetitive work
Other people's safety motivates you
